extracted.intended_audience: students preparing for mathematical olympiads / advanced problem-solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of problem-solving strategies and tactical rules (graph-theory tools, infinite descent, working backwards, conjugates, floor/ceiling manipulations, geometric interpretations of algebraic systems) aimed at solving olympiad-style problems. The page explains each strategy, gives illustrative examples, and lists practice problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph-theory modeling and vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent combinatorial problems as graphs or digraphs: vertices = objects/participants, edges = relations; use notions of connectedness, trees (connected acyclic graphs), cycles, oriented edges (digraphs), degree (valency) of a vertex; represent mappings/permutations as digraphs which split into cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model mappings as arrows from a to f(a); fixed points are points with arrow to themselves. Typical uses: apply parity/degree arguments, cycle structure of permutations, and the box principle in combinatorial problems. Many problems in this section belong to the box principle or standard graph arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing / matching (symmetry) response strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition the board/set into disjoint pairs (x,x) so that whenever the opponent acts on one element of a pair, you respond by acting on the other element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a simple symmetry-winning strategy: e.g., Fig. 13.3 shows a winning partition for B into pairs; if A colors an element of a pair, B colors the other element. Applicable whenever a pairing covers all moves and the second player can mirror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force coefficient-sum zero to make 1 a root (polynomial tactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing/playing with polynomial coefficients in a move sequence, choose the final move so that the sum of coefficients becomes zero, thereby forcing x=1 to be a root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: After three steps three coefficients a,b,c appear; replace the fourth star by −a−b−c−1 so the coefficients sum to zero and hence 1 is a root. Use in constructive/avoidance problems involving polynomial roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction/EUCLID-style game winning criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze two-pile subtraction games by comparing sizes: positions (a,b) with a≥2b are winning for the player to move because one can reduce to a losing position via (a,b)→(a−qb,b) moves; use ratio thresholds α separating winning/losing regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If (a−b,b) is losing then move there; otherwise there exists a q with (a−qb,b) losing; deploy that q. Use bounds on ratios (e.g., α between 1 and 2) and arguments counting possible moves to classify positions without enumerating full strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal-lowest-row marking strategy (grid covering games)
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain marking/covering games on a rectangular board, always play in the lowest (furthest-out) diagonal row that still has free cells. If some cells in that diagonal have a unique cover, mark one of those first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb: restrict moves to the minimal-index diagonal available; when a cell can be covered in two ways it matters less which you choose. This ensures control of covering opportunities and steers the game to a win (used in problem 35).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity/product-vertex argument in graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider products (±1) associated to edges/vertices and use parity/counting to deduce existence of a vertex with a given product sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If every edge contribution is counted twice when multiplying over all vertices, the total product is +1; with an odd number of vertices not all vertex-products can be −1 (since (−1)odd = −1), so at least one vertex has product +1. Use divisibility/ parity of number of vertices and edge-contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite Descent (descending-minimal-counterexample) method
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove impossibility of integer solutions, assume a solution exists, then construct a strictly smaller positive integer solution; iterate to obtain an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic use: show parities force both variables even, divide by 2 to get a smaller solution, repeat. Examples: Pythagorean pentagram rationality argument (E1), no regular n-gon with lattice points for many n (E2) via decreasing side lengths, and diophantine equations of form x^2+... = 2xyzu (E3). The method suits problems where an algebraic manipulation produces smaller integer solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working Backwards (reverse construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the desired final object exists and step backwards to the initial data, reducing possibilities at each backstep. Work backwards when the backward step has few branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when each backward step has only a few possible predecessors so you can reconstruct or derive contradictions. Closely related to infinite descent and used in geometric constructions and functional inversions (Jacobi's dictum: always invert). Illustrated by many problems where assuming existence leads to a unique or few predecessor states until contradiction or construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugate-number technique / rationalizing denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat numbers of the form a + b√r (or more general nested radicals) as elements of quadratic (or higher) field extensions; use conjugates a ± b√r to rationalize denominators and exploit closure of {a + b√r : a,b∈Q} under +,−,·,:.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationalize by multiplying numerator and denominator by conjugates (possibly several factors for higher-degree nested roots). Example trick: multiply (1/(√2+√3)) by product of all sign-choices of conjugates to get a rational denominator; recognize when to square/halve exponents to embed into a+b√n form. Use fields language: these sets are fields, closed under arithmetic, so conjugation maps leave rational expressions invariant in structured ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric interpretation of algebraic systems (use geometry to avoid solving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate algebraic systems into geometric relations (Pythagoras, cosine rule, areas) to find desired symmetric expressions rather than solving for all variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: given x^2 + xy + (y^2)/3 = 25, t^2 + z^2 = 9, z^2 + zx + x^2 = 16, set t = y/√3 and see each equation as a side/angle relation of triangles; use cosine rule and area formulas to compute xy+2yz+3zx directly. Look for known numerical patterns (9,16,25) suggesting right triangles or cosine angles (120°,150°).

rubrics_metrics.name: Floor and ceiling (integer-part) rules and elimination strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and key identities for floor ⌊x⌋ and ceiling ⌈x⌉: ⌊x⌋ = largest integer ≤ x, ⌈x⌉ = least integer ≥ x; useful algebraic relations and inequalities like ⌊x+n⌋ = ⌊x⌋ + n and ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ ⌊x+y⌋. Strategy: eliminate brackets where possible to simplify inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work via decomposition x = ⌊x⌋ + {x} with 0 ≤ {x} < 1 to prove inequalities; be wary that ⌊n x⌋ is not generally equal to n⌊x⌋ (only ⌊n x⌋ ≥ n⌊x⌋). Many combinatorial/number-theory identities (e.g., divisor sums expressed as sums of floors) and contest problems rely on these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lattice polygon / vector-iteration infinite-descent technique
rubrics_metrics.description: To show nonexistence of regular n-gons with integer-lattice vertices for many n, replace the polygon by the polygon formed by successive side-vectors; the new polygon has integral squared side lengths that strictly decrease at each step, yielding an infinite descent contradiction unless n is special (3,4,6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example E2: use the set Z×Z and vector endpoints to form an inner regular n-gon of lattice points; iterating yields smaller integral squared edge lengths ad infinitum, impossible, so conclude impossibility. Combine geometry with integrality of squared distances and area arguments (e.g., triangle area irrationality vs lattice polygons).
